skeleton.note: coordinating conjunction 'and', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: и isn't just 'and then' — it's the basic coordinating conjunction for simply listing people or things together.

grammarFocus.construction: Zero-copula present tense (быть omitted)
grammarFocus.note: 'To be' is omitted in the present tense. Я и ты здесь. simply places the subjects side by side with no verb.

variations.note: A more compact form using the plural pronoun мы.
Same structure with third-person subjects (still no verb).

options.note: Makes 'both of us' explicit.
A natural colloquial way to combine 'me and you.'

paraphrases.simplest: Мы здесь. — the simplest, most everyday phrasing.

takeaway.note: A standard pattern for 'you and I,' far more natural in speech than a literal translation.

skeleton.note: preposition, governs the prepositional case for location

keyPoint: The preposition в governs the prepositional case when expressing location (в городе = 'in the city').

grammarFocus.construction: в + prepositional case
grammarFocus.note: The preposition в ('in') for location takes the prepositional case. городе is the prepositional form of город.

variations.note: Changing the place still gives the prepositional form деревне.

Using находиться sounds more formal/written.

paraphrases.simplest: Я в городе. — the most concise in conversation.

takeaway.note: The most frequent pattern for 'being inside' somewhere — essential for в Москве, в школе, etc.

skeleton.note: negation particle, placed right before the verb

keyPoint: The negation particle не always goes directly before the verb.

grammarFocus.construction: не + verb (negation)

A more direct 'Who are you?'

paraphrases.simplest: Я тебя не знаю. — the simplest, most direct phrasing.

takeaway.note: The most basic negation pattern in Russian — just place не right before the verb.

skeleton.note: preposition, governs the accusative for destination
accusative of стол (hard-declension masculine = same as nominative)

keyPoint: на governs the accusative when expressing a destination (на стол = 'onto the table').

grammarFocus.construction: на + accusative case (destination)
grammarFocus.note: When на marks where something is being placed (destination), it takes the accusative. на стол expresses motion 'onto' the table.

variations.note: If addressing a woman, the past tense is положила.

options.note: Drops the verb and asks about the resulting state (на + prepositional here).
поставить ('to stand something up') is a near-synonymous way to say it.

paraphrases.simplest: Чашка на столе? — most natural when you only care about the result.

takeaway.note: Key point: на стол is 'onto the table' (destination), на столе is 'on the table' (resulting location).

keyPoint: я is always lowercase in Russian, even mid-sentence — the basic first-person singular pronoun.

grammarFocus.construction: Zero-copula noun sentence
grammarFocus.note: 'I am your friend' has no быть — the subject Я and the complement друг sit directly next to each other.

variations.note: If the speaker is female, друг becomes подруга.

options.note: Conveys 'I'm on your side' without naming 'friend' directly.
Directly conveys reassurance: 'you can trust me.'

paraphrases.simplest: Я твой друг. — the plainest, most direct phrasing.

takeaway.note: A basic pattern for declaring your relationship to someone — match твой/твоя to the noun's gender.

keyPoint: быть's present tense is usually dropped, but its past tense (был/была/было/были) is always spelled out.

grammarFocus.construction: Past tense of быть (был/была/было/были)
grammarFocus.note: Быть is dropped in the present but shows up in the past. был is the masculine singular past form.

options.note: Using ходить ('to go') emphasizes the trip rather than just presence.
Same sentence, reordered to emphasize вчера.

paraphrases.simplest: Я был там вчера. — the standard word order, most natural.

takeaway.note: Getting these four gender/number forms of 'was/were' right is the key point.

skeleton.note: interrogative pronoun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: что is the basic interrogative pronoun for asking 'what'.

grammarFocus.construction: Question with что
grammarFocus.note: The question word что ('what') opens the sentence, followed by the verb (2nd person singular present делаешь) — the basic question structure.

options.note: A more colloquial way to ask using заниматься ('to be occupied with').
Shifts to 'what's going on' — asking about the whole situation.

paraphrases.simplest: Что ты делаешь? — the standard phrasing that fits any context.

takeaway.note: An extremely common everyday 'what are you up to?' greeting-style question.

keyPoint: он refers to a male person (or any grammatically masculine inanimate noun).

grammarFocus.construction: Third-person pronoun он + zero-copula sentence
grammarFocus.note: The subject он is followed directly by the complement друг, with no быть.

variations.note: Female subject она: друг becomes подруга.
Plural subject они: друг becomes друзья.

options.note: Emphasizes the mutual relationship.
States acquaintance first, then adds the relationship.

paraphrases.simplest: Он мой друг. — the simplest, most direct phrasing.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for introducing people — match мой/моя to the noun's gender.

keyPoint: с + instrumental expresses 'together with'.

grammarFocus.construction: с + instrumental case
grammarFocus.note: The preposition с ('together with') takes the instrumental case; тобой is the instrumental form of ты.

options.note: Adds рядом ('nearby') to stress physical closeness.
Adds здесь to emphasize location.

paraphrases.simplest: Я с тобой. — dropping сейчас keeps it just as clear and shorter.

takeaway.note: The basic 'together with' pattern — worth memorizing pronoun instrumental forms (тобой, ней, ним, etc.).

skeleton.note: contrastive conjunction, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: а marks a plain contrast between two clauses ('this is X, while that is Y').

grammarFocus.construction: Contrastive conjunction а
grammarFocus.note: А marks a mild contrast ('whereas'), weaker than и, linking тут and там here.

options.note: Replaces the colloquial тут with the more standard здесь.

options.ru: Мы в разных местах: я тут, ты там.
options.note: A more explanatory version that states the situation first.

paraphrases.simplest: Я тут, а ты там. — most natural and concise in speech.

takeaway.note: A very frequent pattern for a mild contrast ('X, but/while Y') — note it's weaker than и's full contrast.

skeleton.note: interrogative adverb 'how', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: Ты как? is a casual fixed phrase for 'how's it going?'.

grammarFocus.construction: как + short confirmation question
grammarFocus.note: Ты как? is a colloquial fixed phrase meaning 'how are you,' omitting the verb — an elliptical structure.

options.note: A softer impersonal way to ask the same thing.
Adding хорошо hints at the expected answer.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты как, выспался? — the most natural way to check in on someone.

takeaway.note: An extremely common fixed phrase for checking on someone's state first.

skeleton.note: demonstrative, 'this' before a noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: это isn't only the pronoun 'this' — right before a noun it also works adjectivally, meaning 'this (particular)'.

grammarFocus.construction: это as the subject, with an embedded question
grammarFocus.note: Это ('this') functions as the subject here: Ты знаешь, это кафе работает? is an embedded question — 'do you know (whether) this café is open?'

options.note: Drops Ты знаешь, for a more direct question.
Drops это and adds сейчас to stress the current state.

paraphrases.simplest: Это кафе работает? — the most concise when you just want to ask directly.

takeaway.note: A very useful lead-in for 'do you happen to know...?'-style confirmation questions.

keyPoint: ты is the informal second-person singular pronoun used with close acquaintances.

grammarFocus.construction: Subject pronoun ты for emphasis
grammarFocus.note: Ты это знаешь? foregrounds ты, emphasizing 'do YOU know this?'

options.note: Using известный ('known') for a more formal register.
The colloquial fixed phrase быть в курсе ('to be in the know').

paraphrases.simplest: Ты это знаешь? — the most standard, simple phrasing.

takeaway.note: A very colloquial alternative for 'do you know?'

skeleton.note: preposition 'toward', governs the dative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: к + dative marks heading toward a person's place.

grammarFocus.construction: к + dative case
grammarFocus.note: The directional preposition к ('toward') takes the dative case; тебе is the dative form of ты.

options.note: The perfective приду makes the future intent explicit (a single upcoming arrival).
Dropping the subject Я for a more colloquial exclamation.

paraphrases.simplest: Иду к тебе! — the most concise declaration in conversation.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for moving toward a person — worth memorizing pronoun dative forms (тебе, вам, etc.).

skeleton.note: adversative conjunction, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: но marks a strong 'but/however' contrast.

grammarFocus.construction: но marking a sharp contrast
grammarFocus.note: Но ('but') signals a clear contradiction, here linking the conflicting feelings хочу and не могу.

variations.note: Female speaker, past tense: хотела/не могла.

options.ru: Я бы хотел, но не получается.
options.note: The conditional бы хотел is more polite/tentative.
Drops the subject and uses the colloquial выходить ('to work out').

paraphrases.simplest: Хочу, но не могу. — dropping the subject gives the most natural colloquial form.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for a sharp contrast ('X, but Y') — note it's stronger than а.

skeleton.note: third-person plural pronoun, subject, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: они is a gender-neutral third-person plural pronoun.

grammarFocus.construction: Third-person plural они + zero-copula sentence
grammarFocus.note: The subject они is followed directly by the plural complement друзья, with no быть.

variations.note: Addressing them directly with the formal/plural вы.

options.note: Groups everyone together as one unit.
States acquaintance first.

paraphrases.simplest: Они мои друзья. — the simplest, most direct phrasing.

takeaway.note: Introducing multiple people — note the irregular plural друг → друзья.

skeleton.note: first-person plural pronoun, subject, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: мы is 'we', always including the speaker.

grammarFocus.construction: Zero-copula sentence with вместе
grammarFocus.note: Мы здесь вместе. omits быть, with the adverb вместе ('together') supplying the extra meaning.

options.note: Makes 'both of us' explicit.
Drops вместе and uses с тобой to convey togetherness instead.

paraphrases.simplest: Мы здесь вместе. — already the simplest phrasing.

takeaway.note: An extremely common adverb for togetherness — works at the end of nearly any sentence regardless of a verb's presence.

skeleton.note: preposition 'behind/after', governs the instrumental, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: за + instrumental means 'following behind'.

grammarFocus.construction: Imperative + за + instrumental case
grammarFocus.note: After the imperative Иди, the preposition за ('behind, after') takes the instrumental; мной is the instrumental form of я.

variations.note: The person to follow changed to third-person ним.

options.note: следовать ('to follow') makes the meaning more explicit.
пойдём turns it into an invitation to go together.

paraphrases.simplest: Иди за мной. — the shortest, most direct command.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for 'following someone' — worth memorizing the pronoun instrumental forms.

skeleton.note: formal/plural second-person pronoun, subject, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: вы is the polite form for one person, or 'you all' for a group.

grammarFocus.construction: Formal/plural second person вы
grammarFocus.note: Вы covers both formal 'you' (singular) and plural 'you all'; the verb always takes the plural form, e.g. понимаете.

variations.note: A single close addressee: ты понимаешь.

options.note: 'Is everything clear to you?' — a different way to check understanding.
Shifts the focus to whether the speaker is explaining clearly.

paraphrases.simplest: Вы меня понимаете? — a standard, ready-to-use question.

takeaway.note: A key Russian-specific pattern: the same form covers both formal singular and plural 'you.'

skeleton.note: preposition 'along', governs the dative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: по + dative expresses moving 'along' a path.

grammarFocus.construction: по + dative case
grammarFocus.note: The preposition по ('along') takes the dative case; улице is the dative form of улица.

options.note: Using гулять ('to stroll') shifts to an aimless walk.
A simpler statement just of location, 'on the street.'

paraphrases.simplest: Мы на улице. — most concise when movement doesn't matter.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for movement along a street or road.

skeleton.note: pronoun 'everything', accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: всё ('everything', things) and все ('everyone', people) look similar but are different pronouns.

grammarFocus.construction: всё + perfective приготовил
grammarFocus.note: Всё ('everything,' neuter) combines with the perfective приготовил ('finished preparing') to ask 'did you finish preparing everything?'

options.note: Using the adjective готов ('ready') for a shorter check.
закончить ('to finish') stresses the completion of the action.

paraphrases.simplest: Всё готово? — the shortest, most everyday way to check.

takeaway.note: An extremely common phrase for checking everything's ready.

skeleton.note: adverb 'that much', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: так is the basic adverb for 'this/that way' or a degree 'that much'.

grammarFocus.construction: так intensifying degree
grammarFocus.note: Так ('so, that much') is a degree adverb modifying любишь ('love').

options.note: нравиться ('to like') is a more general way to put it.
обожать ('to adore') states the strong preference more directly.

paraphrases.simplest: Тебе нравится кофе? — dropping так gives the plainest question.

takeaway.note: A frequent pattern for emphasizing degree, 'so (much)...'

skeleton.note: emphatic particle 'right?', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: же adds a confirming 'right?' nuance to a statement.

grammarFocus.construction: Emphatic particle же
grammarFocus.note: Же adds a tone of 'right?, after all' confirmation, placed right after the word it emphasizes (here, ты).

options.note: ведь ('after all, surely') is nearly synonymous.
точно ('for sure') strengthens the sense of checking.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты помнишь это? — the plain question with же dropped.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent particle adding a 'right?, after all' confirming nuance.

skeleton.note: preposition 'from', governs the genitive, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: от + genitive marks the cause/source of tiredness ('from work').

grammarFocus.construction: от + genitive case (cause)
grammarFocus.note: The preposition от ('from, because of') marking the cause of fatigue takes the genitive case; работы is the genitive form of работа.

options.note: Using утомить ('to tire out') makes 'work' the grammatical subject.
Drops от работы and just asks about the degree of tiredness.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты устал? — dropping от работы gives the plainest question.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for 'because of, from' a cause.

skeleton.note: preposition 'at/by', governs the genitive, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: у + genitive + есть builds Russian's distinctive possessive construction, 'I have...'.

grammarFocus.construction: у + genitive (possession construction)
grammarFocus.note: Possession in Russian is expressed as 'у + the person's genitive + есть + the thing.' Меня is the genitive form of я — literally 'by me there is coffee.'

variations.note: Turned into a question addressed to someone.

options.note: Drops есть for a shorter, colloquial form.
Using взять ('to take') shows how the coffee was acquired.

paraphrases.simplest: У меня кофе. — dropping есть is the most natural everyday form.

takeaway.note: The single most important pattern for expressing possession — Russian's equivalent of 'to have.'

skeleton.note: preposition 'from (inside)', governs the genitive, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: из marks motion from inside something and governs the genitive.

grammarFocus.construction: из + genitive case
grammarFocus.note: The preposition из ('out of, from') takes the genitive case; дома is the genitive form of дом.

variations.note: Changing the starting point keeps the same genitive structure.

options.note: The perfective вышел emphasizes the completed act of leaving.
уходить ('to leave') stresses the departure itself.

paraphrases.simplest: Я иду из дома. — the simplest phrasing as is.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for a point of origin from inside something — pairs with its antonym в ('into').

skeleton.note: preposition 'about', governs the prepositional, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: о + prepositional expresses 'about/concerning'.

grammarFocus.construction: о + prepositional case
grammarFocus.note: The preposition о ('about') takes the prepositional case; работе is the prepositional form of работа.

variations.note: Changed the object to a person (тебе, prepositional of ты).

options.note: беспокоить ('to worry') adds a note of anxiety rather than neutral thought.

options.ru: У меня в голове только работа.
options.note: A more emphatic 'work is all I can think about.'

paraphrases.simplest: Я думаю о работе. — the most standard, plain phrasing.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for the topic of thought/speech — essential for думать о чём, говорить о чём, etc.

skeleton.note: conditional particle, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: бы + a past-tense verb builds the polite hedge 'I would like...'.

grammarFocus.construction: Conditional particle бы + past tense verb
grammarFocus.note: бы + past tense forms a polite, tentative wish. Я бы хотел reads as 'I would like.'

options.note: Dropping бы makes it a more direct, casual statement.
A polite, fixed phrase for ordering: 'May I have coffee?'

paraphrases.simplest: Можно мне кофе? — the most natural phrasing when ordering, e.g. at a café.

takeaway.note: A very frequent tentative-wish pattern, equivalent to English 'I'd like.'

skeleton.note: preposition 'up to', governs the genitive, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: до + genitive marks an endpoint, 'as far as'.

grammarFocus.construction: до + genitive case (destination)
grammarFocus.note: The preposition до ('as far as, up to') takes the genitive case; дома is the genitive form of дом. Дойти is the perfective 'to reach (on foot).'

variations.note: Changing the destination keeps the same genitive structure.

options.note: добраться ('to get somewhere') doesn't specify the means of travel.
Shifts to asking about the distance itself.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты дойдёшь до дома? — the simplest phrasing as is.

takeaway.pattern: до + genitive ('up to, as far as')
takeaway.note: The basic pattern for a destination point — pairs with от ('from') as its antonym.

skeleton.note: a variant of the preposition в, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: во is the form в takes before a consonant cluster.

grammarFocus.construction: во сколько (fixed phrase for time)
grammarFocus.note: Во is a phonetic variant of в before consonant clusters; во сколько is a fixed phrase meaning 'at what time.'

options.note: когда ('when') is a broader question not tied to a specific time.
A more formal/literary way to ask 'at what hour.'

paraphrases.simplest: Во сколько ты придёшь? — the standard way to ask for a specific time.

takeaway.note: An extremely common fixed phrase for 'at what time...?'

skeleton.note: preposition 'for', governs the genitive, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: для + genitive marks a beneficiary, 'for (someone)'.

grammarFocus.construction: для + genitive case
grammarFocus.note: The preposition для ('for') takes the genitive case; мамы is the genitive form of мама.

options.note: Using the dative (маме) for the indirect object is more natural in speech than для + genitive.
Asks about an already-bought gift instead.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты купил маме подарок? — the dative construction is more natural in everyday speech.

takeaway.note: Key point: both для + genitive and the plain dative can express 'for someone.'

skeleton.note: conditional conjunction, this sentence's target word
first-person plural present of идти (hortative use)

keyPoint: если means 'if' and introduces a condition.

grammarFocus.construction: если (conditional clause) + идём (inviting present)
grammarFocus.note: Если ('if') introduces the condition, and идём (literally 1st person plural present of 'to go') functions here as 'let's go.'

options.note: The perfective пойдём makes the single upcoming departure clearer.
Drops если and uses a dash for a more colloquial link.

paraphrases.simplest: Если хочешь, идём. — already the most natural phrasing.

takeaway.note: The basic conditional conjunction 'if' — very frequently combined with the inviting идём/пойдём.

skeleton.note: interrogative adverb 'when', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: когда asks 'when', and also works as the conjunction 'when (something happens)'.

grammarFocus.construction: когда (question word) + perfective future придёшь
grammarFocus.note: Когда ('when') opens the sentence, combined with the perfective future придёшь ('will arrive') to ask 'when will you come?'

options.note: Asks for a more specific time.
скоро ('soon') asks for a rough sense of timing.

paraphrases.simplest: Когда ты придёшь? — the standard way to ask about timing.

takeaway.note: The most frequent question-word pattern for asking 'when.'

skeleton.note: purpose conjunction, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: чтобы + infinitive expresses purpose, 'in order to' (when the subject is the same).

grammarFocus.construction: чтобы + infinitive (purpose)
grammarFocus.note: Чтобы ('in order to') is followed by an infinitive; помочь is the infinitive of помочь.

options.note: Drops чтобы — the perfective пришёл can take an infinitive directly.
A more noun-based phrasing using помощь ('help').

paraphrases.simplest: Я пришёл помочь. — works just as well without чтобы, and is more concise.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for stating purpose.

skeleton.note: disjunctive conjunction, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: или expresses 'or', a choice between options.

grammarFocus.construction: или (disjunctive conjunction)
grammarFocus.note: Или means 'or,' here linking two choices: чай (tea) and кофе (coffee).

options.note: Dropping subject and verb is very natural when taking an order.

options.ru: Что будешь пить, чай или кофе?
options.note: A more polite way that first asks what they'd like to drink.

paraphrases.simplest: Чай или кофе? — the most natural phrasing at a café or restaurant.

takeaway.note: The basic 'X or Y' pattern — extremely frequent when offering a choice.

skeleton.note: question particle, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: ли comes right after the verb to form a yes/no question, including inside indirect questions.

grammarFocus.construction: Interrogative particle ли
grammarFocus.note: Ли is a literary interrogative particle placed right after the verb; Знаешь ли ты это? forms a slightly formal yes/no question.

options.note: Dropping ли gives a more colloquial, natural question.
Adding интересно ('interesting') softens it into something closer to musing aloud.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты это знаешь? — dropping ли is the most natural everyday phrasing.

takeaway.note: A somewhat formal particle used in literary/indirect questions — often dropped in everyday speech.

skeleton.note: place adverb 'there', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: там is the basic adverb for 'there'.

grammarFocus.construction: там ('there,' adverb of place) + past of быть
grammarFocus.note: Там ('there') combines with был (masculine singular past of быть) to express 'was there.'

options.note: ходить + туда ('to there') emphasizes the trip itself.
Same sentence reordered to stress вчера.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты был там вчера? — the standard word order, most natural.

takeaway.note: The basic adverb for 'there' — pairs with здесь/тут ('here') as its antonym.

skeleton.note: colloquial place adverb 'here', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: тут is a colloquial synonym of здесь.

grammarFocus.construction: тут ('here,' colloquial adverb) + уже ('already')
grammarFocus.note: Тут is nearly synonymous with здесь ('here') but sounds more colloquial. Уже means 'already.'

variations.note: Replaces the colloquial тут with the more standard здесь.

options.note: пришёл (perfective 'arrived') conveys the fact of having arrived.
вот ('here, look') gives a very colloquial 'here I am.'

paraphrases.simplest: Я уже тут. — already the most colloquial, natural form.

takeaway.note: Тут is a more colloquial version of здесь — essentially the same meaning, different register.

skeleton.note: place adverb 'here', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: здесь is the basic adverb for 'here'.

grammarFocus.construction: здесь ('here,' standard adverb)
grammarFocus.note: Здесь is the most neutral, standard word for 'here,' usable in both speech and writing, unlike the more colloquial тут.

options.note: Drops the verb and asks about the resulting state.
забыть ('to forget') shifts to an unintentional leaving-behind.

paraphrases.simplest: Телефон здесь? — the most concise when you only care about the result.

takeaway.note: The most standard adverb for 'here' — usable across a wider range of contexts than тут, including formal writing.

skeleton.note: interrogative adverb 'where', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: где asks about location.

grammarFocus.construction: где (question word, location)
grammarFocus.note: Где ('where') asks about location, placed at the start of the sentence.

options.note: Switching to куда ('where to,' direction) asks about a destination instead — note the где/куда distinction.
A more colloquial, casual word order.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты где? — the most common casual phrasing, e.g. on the phone.

takeaway.note: The key point is distinguishing где (static location) from куда (direction).

skeleton.note: interrogative pronoun 'who', this sentence's target word

keyPoint: кто asks 'who' and grammatically always takes masculine singular agreement.

grammarFocus.construction: Embedded question with кто

options.note: Drops Ты знаешь, for a more direct question.
Shifts focus to identifying the person rather than the action.

paraphrases.simplest: Кто пришёл? — the most concise when you just want to know.

takeaway.note: An important rule: кто always takes masculine singular verb agreement, regardless of gender.

skeleton.note: determiner 'all/whole', masculine singular, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: весь is a universal determiner that inflects for gender/number/case — a different word from the pronoun всё.

grammarFocus.construction: весь + accusative (duration)
grammarFocus.note: Весь ('whole') with a duration noun like день takes the accusative with no preposition, expressing 'all day.'

options.note: целый ('entire') is nearly synonymous.
Shifts from past tense to a statement of the state itself.

paraphrases.simplest: Я работал весь день. — the most standard phrasing as is.

takeaway.note: The preposition-free accusative for a whole span of time — same structure as весь год, всю неделю, etc.

skeleton.note: reflexive possessive determiner, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: свой is the reflexive possessive, referring back to the subject itself.

grammarFocus.construction: Reflexive possessive свой
grammarFocus.note: Свой refers back to the subject's own possession, and the same word свой is used regardless of whether the subject is я, он, они, etc.

variations.note: Свой stays свой even with a third-person subject.

options.note: Мой is also possible here, but with less emphasis than свой.
Using нравиться gives a more general 'I like' phrasing.

paraphrases.simplest: Я люблю свой город. — already the most natural phrasing.

takeaway.note: A key determiner that refers back to the subject's own possession, regardless of the subject's person.

skeleton.note: possessive determiner, first-person plural, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: наш marks possession by a group including the speaker.

grammarFocus.construction: Possessive наш (inanimate accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Because столик is inanimate, наш (our) in the accusative looks identical to its nominative form (наш столик).

options.note: Asks directly 'where is our table?'
заметить ('to notice') is a close alternative.

paraphrases.simplest: Где наш столик? — most practical when looking for a seat.

takeaway.note: The plural-owner possessive — note the inanimate accusative = nominative rule.

skeleton.note: formal possessive determiner, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: ваш is the formal/plural 'your'.

grammarFocus.construction: Formal possessive ваш inside a quoted construction
grammarFocus.note: Ваш ('your,' formal) appears here inside direct quotation marks «...» — a polite phrase a staff member might say to a customer.

variations.note: Subject changed to third person (a different speaker).

options.note: Drops ваш for a more concise confirmation.
Among friends, твой replaces the formal ваш.

paraphrases.simplest: Заказ готов? — the most concise phrasing in a casual setting.

takeaway.note: Essential in polite service contexts — note the твой/ваш distinction for casual vs. formal.

skeleton.note: possessive determiner, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: мой is the first-person singular possessive, agreeing with its noun's gender/number/case.

grammarFocus.construction: Possessive мой (inanimate accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Because телефон is inanimate, мой ('my') in the accusative matches its nominative form (мой телефон).

options.note: Asks about location directly rather than whether it's been found.
Directly checks whether the other person has it.

paraphrases.simplest: Где мой телефон? — most practical when searching for a lost item.

takeaway.note: The most frequent possessive — note the inanimate accusative = nominative rule.

skeleton.note: informal possessive determiner, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: твой marks possession by someone you address informally.

grammarFocus.construction: Possessive твой (inanimate accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Because подарок is inanimate, твой ('your,' informal) in the accusative matches its nominative form (твой подарок).

options.note: Asks about location directly.
The reflexive нашёлся ('turned up') gives a more spontaneous nuance.

paraphrases.simplest: Где твой подарок? — most practical when searching for a lost item.

takeaway.note: The informal possessive for someone close — switch to ваш for a formal addressee.

skeleton.note: possessive determiner 'his', indeclinable, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: его ('his') is an indeclinable possessive, identical in form to он's genitive.

replies.gloss: Yeah, I know it by heart.

grammarFocus.construction: Invariant possessive его
grammarFocus.note: Его ('his') never changes form regardless of the gender, number, or case of the noun it modifies — it's fixed, derived from the owner's own gender.

variations.note: Changing the owner to feminine gives её ('her'), but it's equally invariant.

options.note: Asks directly 'what's his number?'
Shifts to asking whether you can reach him, rather than whether you remember the number.

paraphrases.simplest: Какой у него номер? — most practical when you just want the number itself.

takeaway.note: The key point: его, её, and их never change form no matter the gender, number, or case of the noun they modify.

skeleton.note: possessive determiner 'her', indeclinable, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: её ('her') is an indeclinable possessive determiner.

grammarFocus.construction: Invariant possessive её
grammarFocus.note: Её ('her') stays the same form regardless of the modified noun's gender, number, or case, just like его and их.

options.note: The standard fixed phrase for 'what's her name?'
Using известный ('known') gives a more formal phrasing.

paraphrases.simplest: Как её зовут? — the most standard way to ask someone's name.

takeaway.note: An extremely common fixed phrase for asking 'what is his/her name?'

skeleton.note: possessive determiner 'their', indeclinable, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: их ('their') is an indeclinable possessive determiner.

grammarFocus.construction: Invariant possessive их
grammarFocus.note: Их ('their') also stays the same form regardless of the modified noun's gender, number, or case, just like его and её.

options.note: A direct 'what's their last name?'
Using известный ('known') gives a more formal phrasing.

paraphrases.simplest: Как их фамилия? — the most standard, simple way to ask.

takeaway.note: Worth memorizing as a set: all three third-person possessives are invariant.

skeleton.note: reflexive pronoun, accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: себя is a reflexive pronoun with no nominative form — it always appears in an oblique case.

grammarFocus.construction: чувствовать себя + instrumental (state expression)
grammarFocus.note: Себя ('oneself,' reflexive accusative) is used in the fixed phrase чувствовать себя; the following state word (here an adverb, плохо) describes how one feels.

options.note: A shorter impersonal way to say you feel unwell.
неважно ('not great') softens it a bit.

paraphrases.simplest: Мне плохо. — the shortest, most everyday way to say you feel unwell.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent pattern for 'to feel (a certain way)' — себя itself never changes form.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: друг is a masculine noun with an irregular plural, друзья.

grammarFocus.construction: Zero-copula sentence with adjective agreement
grammarFocus.note: Мой ('my') and хороший ('good') both agree with друг (a masculine noun); быть is absent.

variations.note: For a female addressee: подруга, and хорошая agrees.

options.note: отличный ('excellent') gives a stronger compliment.
Using дружба ('friendship') evaluates the relationship itself.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты хороший друг. — dropping мой gives a shorter version.

takeaway.note: In Russian, adjectives and possessives must always agree with the noun's gender, number, and case.

skeleton.note: masculine noun, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: the plural of человек is not человеки but the suppletive form люди.

grammarFocus.construction: человек (always grammatically masculine) + adjective agreement
grammarFocus.note: Человек ('person') is always grammatically masculine regardless of the referent's actual gender, so хороший (masculine) agrees.

variations.note: Still хороший человек even with a formal addressee.
Same form with a third-person subject.

options.note: 'You have a kind heart' — a more figurative compliment.
добрый ('kind') alone is a shorter compliment.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты хороший. — dropping человек gives a shorter version.

takeaway.note: The key point: человек stays grammatically masculine even when describing a woman.

skeleton.note: demonstrative determiner, masculine accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: этот is a demonstrative determiner that inflects for gender/number/case, unlike the invariant pronoun это.

grammarFocus.construction: Demonstrative этот (inanimate accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Because столик is inanimate, этот ('this') in the accusative matches its nominative form (этот столик).

options.note: нравиться ('to like') shifts toward the reason for the choice.
Using садиться ('to sit down') is a more action-oriented suggestion.

paraphrases.simplest: Садимся здесь? — most practical when deciding where to sit.

takeaway.note: The basic demonstrative for something nearby — note the inanimate accusative = nominative rule.

skeleton.note: demonstrative determiner, masculine accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: тот means "that (far)" and pairs with этот "this (near)".

grammarFocus.construction: Demonstrative тот (inanimate accusative = nominative)
grammarFocus.note: Because вечер is inanimate, тот ('that') in the accusative matches its nominative form (тот вечер).

variations.note: Changing the noun to день keeps the same structure.

options.note: тогда ('back then') avoids naming a specific noun.
Adds особенный ('special') to share the impression of that evening.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты помнишь тот вечер? — the simplest phrasing as is.

takeaway.note: The key distinction between something close by (этот) and something farther off or already mentioned (тот).

skeleton.note: pronoun "everything", accusative, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: всё (everything) is an invariant pronoun, used here as the accusative direct object.

grammarFocus.construction: всё (neuter object pronoun)
grammarFocus.note: Всё ('everything') is a neuter pronoun referring to 'all things/matters,' functioning as the verb's accusative object.

options.note: Using ясно ('clear') in an impersonal construction.
The perfective понял expresses 'have fully understood.'

paraphrases.simplest: Мне всё ясно. — a very natural way to express understanding.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent pronoun for 'everything' — always stays neuter, never changes form.

skeleton.note: negative response particle, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: нет is the basic "no" response particle.

grammarFocus.construction: Negative response particle нет
grammarFocus.note: Нет ('no') negates the response as a whole, separate from the verb negation (не хочу) in the following clause.

options.note: Dropping нет and answering with just the negated verb.
The fixed polite way to decline.

paraphrases.simplest: Нет, спасибо. — the most natural way to politely refuse.

takeaway.note: A two-layer negation pattern: нет to open the answer, then не before the verb within the sentence.

skeleton.note: affirmative response particle, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: да is the basic affirmative particle.

grammarFocus.construction: Affirmative response particle да
grammarFocus.note: Да ('yes') is the basic affirmative particle, with the following clause (я знаю) elaborating on it.

options.note: Dropping да for a shorter affirmation.
Adding конечно ('of course') strengthens the certainty.

paraphrases.simplest: Знаю. — the most concise affirmative response in speech.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern of affirming, then adding supporting detail.

skeleton.note: мочь, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: мочь is an imperfective verb expressing situational ability/possibility.

replies.gloss: Should I put on some music?

grammarFocus.construction: не + мочь + infinitive
grammarFocus.note: Мочь ('to be able') governs an infinitive (спать); negation goes right before мочь itself.

options.note: The impersonal reflexive спится is a more natural, colloquial way to say it.
Using the noun бессонница ('insomnia') is a more clinical way to say it.

paraphrases.simplest: Мне не спится. — very natural when saying you can't sleep.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for 'cannot (do something)' — negation goes before мочь.

keyPoint: сказать is perfective, denoting a single completed act of speaking.

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + perfective infinitive сказать
grammarFocus.note: After что, хочешь ('want') governs the perfective infinitive сказать ('to say, once'), asking 'what are you trying to say?'

options.note: The fixed phrase иметь в виду ('to mean, intend').
A more action-oriented 'please explain.'

paraphrases.simplest: Что ты имеешь в виду? — most natural when checking what someone means.

takeaway.note: An extremely common pattern for checking the intent behind someone's words.

skeleton.note: говорить, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: говорить is imperfective, expressing the ongoing act/ability of speaking.

grammarFocus.construction: говорить (imperfective) + adverb медленно
grammarFocus.note: Говорить is imperfective, expressing the ongoing act of 'speaking,' paired with the perfective сказать. Медленно ('slowly') modifies the manner.

options.note: разговаривать ('to converse,' two-way) is a close alternative.
The comparative помедленнее ('a bit slower') signals an intent to improve.

paraphrases.simplest: Я говорю медленно. — dropping очень gives a shorter version.

takeaway.note: The basic verb for the ongoing act of 'speaking,' paired with the perfective сказать ('to say, once').

keyPoint: знать is an imperfective stative verb.

replies.gloss: Why do you want to know?

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + infinitive знать
grammarFocus.note: Хочу ('want') is followed by the infinitive знать ('to know'). Знать is a stative verb with no clear aspectual pair.

options.note: узнать (perfective, 'to find out') plus интересно ('interesting').
A direct request: 'tell me about it.'

paraphrases.simplest: Расскажи мне об этом. — the most natural request when seeking information.

takeaway.note: The most frequent modal construction for 'wanting to (do something).'

skeleton.note: хотеть, 3rd person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: хотеть has irregular conjugation (singular stem хоч-, plural stem хот-).

grammarFocus.construction: хотеть + infinitive спать
grammarFocus.note: Хочет ('wants') is followed by the infinitive спать ('to sleep') — an extremely common pattern for expressing sleepiness.

options.note: The impersonal reflexive хочется is a more natural way to express the urge.
Adds устал ('tired') and лечь ('to lie down') for more specificity.

paraphrases.simplest: Ему хочется спать. — a very natural way to convey sleepiness.

takeaway.note: The impersonal counterpart хочется is also extremely frequent in everyday speech.

skeleton.note: идти, 2nd person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: идти is the imperfective unidirectional verb of motion.

grammarFocus.construction: куда (directional question word) + идти (unidirectional motion verb)
grammarFocus.note: Куда ('where to') asks about direction, combined with идти (unidirectional, in-progress motion) — distinct from the multidirectional ходить.

options.note: A casual, informal word order, often used in passing.
направляться ('to head toward') is a somewhat more formal way to ask.

paraphrases.simplest: Ты куда? — the most common casual phrasing, e.g. when passing someone.

takeaway.note: The key distinction: идти is one trip in progress right now; ходить is round-trip or habitual.

keyPoint: делать is an imperfective verb of general "doing/making".

grammarFocus.construction: уметь + infinitive делать
grammarFocus.note: Уметь ('to know how to') differs from мочь ('to be able to, circumstantially') — it marks a learned skill. Делать is imperfective, paired with the perfective сделать.

variations.note: готовить ('to prepare') is a close, more specific alternative.

options.note: сварить (perfective, 'to brew') shifts closer to a one-time request.
разбираться ('to be knowledgeable about') asks about expertise more than skill.

paraphrases.simplest: Можешь сварить кофе? — most practical when actually asking someone to make it.

takeaway.note: A key modal distinguishing learned skill (уметь) from circumstantial ability (мочь).

skeleton.note: видеть, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: видеть is an imperfective perception verb; it has no standard imperative.

grammarFocus.construction: видеть (imperfective) + accusative
grammarFocus.note: Видеть is imperfective, expressing the ongoing state of visual perception, paired with the perfective увидеть ('to catch sight of'). Тебя is accusative.

options.note: The perfective заметить ('to notice') marks a single moment of catching sight.
A colloquial exclamation on spotting someone: 'There you are!'

paraphrases.simplest: Вот ты где! — most natural upon finally spotting someone you were looking for.

takeaway.note: The key pair: видеть for ongoing visual perception, увидеть for the momentary 'catch sight of.'

skeleton.note: думать, 1st person singular present, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: думать takes о + prepositional case for "to think about".

grammarFocus.construction: думать (imperfective) + о + prepositional
grammarFocus.note: Думать is imperfective for ongoing thought, paired with подумать. О доме is о + the prepositional form of дом.

options.note: скучать по ('to miss') carries more emotional longing than plain 'thinking.'

options.ru: Дом часто у меня в мыслях.
options.note: A more figurative 'home is often on my mind.'

paraphrases.simplest: Я скучаю по дому. — most natural when expressing homesickness.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for the object of thought — note the distinction from скучать по ('to miss,' + dative).

skeleton.note: restrictive particle "only", this sentence's target word

keyPoint: только is a particle meaning "only".

grammarFocus.construction: только (restrictive particle)
grammarFocus.note: Только ('only') is placed before чай, restricting the choice and excluding any other option.

options.note: просто ('just') is a more natural way to order at a café.
никакого ('none at all') first strongly rejects, then restricts.

paraphrases.simplest: Мне просто чай, спасибо. — the most natural, polite way to order.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent particle for restricting something to one single option.

keyPoint: ещё means "more/still" as an adverb.

grammarFocus.construction: Imperative дай + ещё ('more')
grammarFocus.note: Дай ('give,' imperative) followed by ещё ('more, additional') forms the basic structure for asking for more.

variations.note: Changing the object to вода ('water') keeps the structure.

options.note: можно ('may I') is a more polite way to request.
добавить ('to add') is another phrasing.

paraphrases.simplest: Можно ещё кофе? — the most polite and natural in a restaurant setting.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent pattern for asking for a refill/more of something.

keyPoint: уже means "already", pairing with ещё не ("not yet").

grammarFocus.construction: уже ('already') + дома (adverb of location, no preposition)
grammarFocus.note: Дома ('at home') is a special preposition-free adverb form, distinct from the prepositional доме. Уже marks completion, 'already.'

options.note: The perfective добраться ('arrived') reports the act of arriving itself.
вернуться ('to return,' perfective) is another option.

paraphrases.simplest: Я дома. — dropping уже gives the shortest report.

takeaway.note: Distinguish дома ('at home') from домой ('homeward') and из дома ('from home') — three distinct forms.

keyPoint: очень is the basic intensifying adverb "very".

grammarFocus.construction: очень (degree adverb) + люблю
grammarFocus.note: Очень ('very') modifies люблю ('love'), intensifying the emotion.

variations.note: Dropping очень gives a plainer declaration of love.

options.note: дорог ('dear,' short-form adjective) is a more poetic phrasing.
The idiom без ума от ('crazy about') is a stronger expression of love.

paraphrases.simplest: Я тебя люблю. — this already works well without очень.

takeaway.note: The most frequent adverb for emphasizing emotional intensity or degree.

keyPoint: сейчас is a simple adverb meaning "now".

grammarFocus.construction: сейчас ('now') + работаю (present progressive sense)
grammarFocus.note: Сейчас ('right now') is an adverb; Russian present tense alone covers ongoing action — no separate progressive form is needed.

options.note: A short way to state 'I'm at work.'
Adds занят ('busy') to stress being tied up.

paraphrases.simplest: Я на работе. — very natural when briefly stating your situation.

takeaway.note: The basic adverb for emphasizing an action happening right now.

skeleton.note: adverb "now (as opposed to before)", this sentence's target word

keyPoint: теперь implies a change from how things were before, unlike plain сейчас.

grammarFocus.construction: теперь ('now,' contrastive with the past)
grammarFocus.note: Unlike plain сейчас, теперь implies a contrast with an earlier state — 'now (unlike before).'

variations.note: Switched to the impersonal construction with ясно.

options.note: наконец ('finally') plus the perfective понял stresses the process of arriving at understanding.
Adding а ('ah') captures the moment of realization.

paraphrases.simplest: Теперь понятно. — very natural when expressing a change in understanding.

takeaway.note: A key distinction from сейчас (plain 'now') — теперь implies a change of state.

keyPoint: потом is a temporal adverb meaning "later".

grammarFocus.construction: давай + 1st person plural perfective future (inviting construction)
grammarFocus.note: Давай ('come on, let's') is followed by the perfective future first-person plural form поговорим ('let's talk') — a Russian-specific inviting structure.

options.note: Dropping давай while keeping the verb alone conveys the invitation.
можем ('we can') makes it a more tentative suggestion.

paraphrases.simplest: Поговорим позже? — already quite natural without давай.

takeaway.note: The basic pattern for 'let's (do something)' — equivalent to English 'let's.'

keyPoint: просто means "simply/just", and is also used colloquially as a filler for emphasis.

grammarFocus.construction: просто ('just, simply') + шутишь
grammarFocus.note: Просто ('just') modifies шутишь ('are joking'), adding the nuance of 'just joking, right?'

options.note: да ('right?') carries a similar confirming nuance.
Using the noun шутка ('a joke') is shorter and more direct.

paraphrases.simplest: Это шутка? — the shortest, most direct way to check.

takeaway.note: A frequent adverb for downplaying or restricting the significance of something.

keyPoint: тоже is a colloquial adverb meaning "also/too".

grammarFocus.construction: тоже ('also, too,' agreeing adverb)
grammarFocus.note: Тоже agrees with and adds to a previous statement, typically placed right after the subject or near the end.

options.note: Using и gives a more emphatic 'me too.'
Expresses agreement indirectly as 'count me in.'

paraphrases.simplest: Я тоже хочу. — the simplest phrasing as is.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent pattern for agreeing with or adding to what someone said.

skeleton.note: impersonal predicate of permission, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: можно is an impersonal predicate expressing permission/possibility.

grammarFocus.construction: можно (possibility predicate) + infinitive
grammarFocus.note: Можно ('may, is it okay to') is an impersonal predicate followed by an infinitive (сидеть) — a basic construction for asking permission.

variations.note: здесь replaced with the more colloquial тут.

options.note: свободно ('free') asks about the seat's state directly.
могу ('can I') asks for personal permission.

paraphrases.simplest: Это место свободно? — most practical when looking for a seat.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent impersonal construction for asking permission or possibility.

skeleton.note: necessity predicate, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: надо is a colloquial necessity predicate taking a dative subject.

grammarFocus.construction: надо (necessity predicate) + dative + adverb домой
grammarFocus.note: Надо ('need to') is an impersonal predicate taking a dative subject (мне); домой ('homeward') is a directional adverb.

variations.note: Dative changed to plural нам ('to us').

options.note: пора ('it's time to') adds a sense of urgency.
должен ('must') expresses it as an obligation.

paraphrases.simplest: Мне пора домой. — very natural when announcing you need to leave.

takeaway.note: The basic impersonal construction for 'need to' — the subject is always in the dative.

skeleton.note: necessity predicate, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: нужно is a necessity predicate taking a dative subject.

grammarFocus.construction: нужно (necessity predicate) + infinitive
grammarFocus.note: Нужно ('need to') is an impersonal predicate taking a dative subject, followed by an infinitive (работать). Nearly synonymous with надо.

options.note: Using надо is nearly synonymous.
должен ('must') frames it as an obligation.

paraphrases.simplest: Мне надо работать. — the most natural in conversation.

takeaway.note: Nearly identical to надо — worth learning both.

skeleton.note: prohibitive predicate, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: нельзя is an impersonal predicate expressing prohibition/impossibility.

grammarFocus.construction: нельзя (prohibition predicate) + infinitive
grammarFocus.note: Нельзя ('must not') is an impersonal predicate with an infinitive (делать), expressing a strong prohibition — the negative counterpart of можно.

variations.note: Adding the dative тебе names who the prohibition applies to.

options.note: The negated imperative is a more direct instruction.
The negated стоит ('worth it') softens it into advice.

paraphrases.simplest: Не делай так. — most natural when directly telling someone to stop.

takeaway.note: The basic construction for 'must not' — the antonym of можно ('may').

keyPoint: хорошо is the adverbial form of хороший.

grammarFocus.construction: хорошо (degree adverb) + говоришь
grammarFocus.note: Хорошо ('well') modifies говоришь ('speak'), describing the manner.

options.note: Takes русский ('your Russian') itself as the subject of evaluation.
свободно ('fluently') gives a stronger compliment.

paraphrases.simplest: У тебя хороший русский. — a very natural way to praise someone's language skill.

takeaway.note: An extremely frequent adverb for evaluating ability/skill — pairs with its antonym плохо ('poorly').

keyPoint: плохо is the adverbial form of плохой.

grammarFocus.construction: плохо (degree adverb) + сплю
grammarFocus.note: Плохо ('poorly') modifies сплю ('sleep'), describing the manner. The antonym of хорошо.

options.note: Using сон ('sleep') itself as the subject.
нормально ('normally') gives a more specific complaint.

paraphrases.simplest: Я плохо сплю. — the simplest, standard phrasing.

takeaway.note: A basic antonym pair for evaluating the quality/manner of an action.

skeleton.note: comparative of хорошо, this sentence's target word

keyPoint: лучше is the suppletive comparative of хорошо.

grammarFocus.construction: Comparative лучше (comparative of хорошо)
grammarFocus.note: Лучше ('better') is the irregular comparative of хорошо, following чувствовать себя to mean 'feeling better.'

options.note: легче ('easier,' comparative) is a more colloquial way to ask.
поправляться ('to recover') is a more medical way to ask.

paraphrases.simplest: Тебе легче? — very natural when checking on someone's health.

takeaway.note: The irregular comparative of хорошо — extremely common when asking about improving health/state.

skeleton.note: adverb "any more", this sentence's target word

keyPoint: больше не is an emphatic negative construction meaning "no longer/not any more".

grammarFocus.construction: больше не ('no longer')
grammarFocus.note: Больше ('any more') combines with не to express the end of an action or state.

options.note: хватит ('enough') is a stronger refusal.
передумать ('to change one's mind') directly states the shift.

paraphrases.simplest: Хватит. — the most concise when firmly declining.
